title: Managing Russia’s Military-Industrial Degradation: Navigating Wartime Industrial Constraints, Stockpile Exhaustion, and Hardware Attrition
content:
• This paper assesses Russia’s near-term domestic defense-industrial capacity and the ability of the military-industrial complex (OPK) to meet the increasing demands of the war against Ukraine.
  • Four years into the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Russia has not solved the problem of sustaining wartime production. Instead, the Kremlin has only postponed addressing the OPK’s many problems.
  • Output constraints are increasingly defining the OPK’s future: exhaustion (specifically, the depletion of existing stockpiles and the constant need to repair damaged equipment and refurbish Soviet-legacy hardware taken out of storage) and attrition (the limited ability to produce new military hardware domestically faster than it is consumed).
  • Finding a balance between the two constraints has allowed the armed forces to continue fielding equipment, but it has also accelerated the depletion of Soviet-era reserves. However, the constant trade-off has become a systemic condition that defines the current and future trajectory of the military industry. The OPK cannot indefinitely compensate for battlefield losses through repair and refurbishment alone.
snippet: This paper assesses Russia’s near-term domestic defense-industrial capacity and the ability of the military-industrial complex (OPK) to meet the increasing demands of the war against Ukraine.
creator: Federico Borsari

title: Data Center Attacks Matter But Not in the Way We Thought
content:
Within hours of the attacks, it was claimed the strikes had done something years of counter-disinformation efforts had struggled to achieve by taking Russian propaganda bots offline. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said social media had become easier to navigate, with fewer bots, less division, and fewer provocations. 

Officials pointed to apparent interruptions in Russian automated information networks, while commentators began asking if Ukraine had found a way to physically disrupt the infrastructure underpinning Russia’s information war. 

However, while researchers have found evidence of temporary disruption to some automated Russian networks, there is little evidence that the strikes degraded its broader influence operations.  

Moscow’s information operations include a wide range of tools, including various servers, cloud platforms, and residential internet connections. Moreover, the affected data centers supported a wide range of digital services. The disruptions observed in automated systems cannot be equated with a weakening of the Kremlin’s entire propaganda apparatus.

title: Hybrid War Makes High North a Contest for NATO
content:
This article forms part of a CEPA series on the new strategic landscape in the Arctic.

“High North, low tension” is becoming a comforting slogan rather than a credible strategy. Russia’s war on Ukraine, NATO’s northern enlargement, and growing Russia-China cooperation have eroded Arctic exceptionalism.

A conventional Russia-NATO war is not inevitable, but Moscow is likely to continue using sabotage, cyberattacks, electronic interference, and provocations to challenge sovereignty and test allied resolve. The alliance’s challenge is to defend the High North against aggression deliberately kept below the threshold of war.

Moscow’s Arctic strategy centers on protecting its nuclear deterrent, controlling the Northern Sea Route, and restricting NATO’s access to sensitive Russian territory. The Kola Peninsula, which abuts Norway and Finland and is home to key Northern Fleet and sea-based nuclear assets, is central to these objectives.

The war in Ukraine has weakened some of Russia’s conventional capabilities, while Finland and Sweden’s NATO accession has heightened Moscow’s sense of exposure, a combination that may encourage greater reliance on asymmetric operations.
snippet: This article forms part of a CEPA series on the new strategic landscape in the Arctic.
creator: Sara George

title: Midterm Fallout: AI and Data Centers Take Center Stage
content:
An unpopular war in Iran. Rising prices for gas and groceries. Anger over data centers. These three issues combined to propel the Democrats to a historic midterm victory, raising the prospect that the new Congress will pursue data center moratoriums and AI safety regulation. 

Public pressure for action is mounting. According to exit polling, 56% of voters stated that AI and data centers represented a “crucial or major factor” in their ballot decision. Data centers are blamed for rising electricity bills. Democrats weaponized the issue, spending more than $100 million on ads framing Republicans as friends of data centers. They even sent personalized leaflets to Texas voters near a proposed data center site, warning that Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton would give the project a green light. Paxton lost.

title: Can Congress Narrow the Transatlantic Tech Divide?
content:
European tech policy leaders are cautious.

Democrats won both chambers of Congress, many of whom campaigned on reigning in tech billionaires, curtailing energy-intensive data centers, and imposing artificial intelligence safety rules. These positions could bring US tech policy much closer to Europe’s strict approach.

But European politicians and analysts warned against exaggerated expectations. A lame-duck President Donald Trump retains the key powers over trade, tech, and foreign policy.

“Trump retains extensive foreign policy powers and a legislative veto,” says Javier Carbonell, a policy analyst at the European Policy Center. “His reaction remains unpredictable: domestic constraints could even encourage greater international activism. Europeans should not mistake electoral change for a return to transatlantic normality.”
snippet: European tech policy leaders are cautious.
creator: Bill Echikson

title: Europe’s Sanctions on Russia: Riddled With Loopholes
content:
Over half of the names the EU added to its sanctions in October are aimed at the production chain of the ballistic missiles now targeting Ukrainian cities, chief diplomat Kaja Kallas said. The list of 826 Russian companies and 743 of their chief executives is the EU’s largest-ever set of military-industrial listings. 

A couple of days later, the Council added 12 more names for helping Russia evade sanctions, among them oil intermediaries in the United Arab Emirates and India. 

Yet October avoided the politically difficult decisions. No new sector-wide trade ban, and nothing on oil or gas.  

Europe has two problems with its Russia sanctions: any one of the bloc’s 27 members can insist that its special interests are protected, and the rules already agreed are enforced unevenly. 

July showed how the first problem works. The package passed only after Greece secured an exemption allowing EU operators to carry Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG) to third countries under pre-invasion contracts. A proposed ban on Russian fish imports was dropped along the way. 

Every sector-wide measure affects businesses among the 27 members. Every capital has a veto.

title: Supermarket Attacks: Europe Can’t Wait for Russian Fingerprints
content:
A Belgian butcher is awakened at 3:30 in the morning by an employee reporting a problem with his refrigeration system. When he reaches his shop, temperatures have climbed to 18° Celsius. He estimates that about $17,000 worth of meat has been ruined. Elsewhere in Europe, supermarket workers have discovered similar problems.

The refrigeration attacks were reported in early November, around the same time that European airlines faced a wave of anonymous bomb threats. On the worst day so far, November 5, at least 21 flights had been targeted, prompting diversions, security inspections, and disruption to airline schedules. There is no established connection between the two sets of incidents.​​​ 

​​Supermarket chill cabinets and short-haul airline flights are not what most Europeans picture when they hear about Russia’s shadow war. They think of espionage, cyberattacks against government networks, suspicious fires at defense factories, or damaged infrastructure in the Baltic Sea. These are serious threats, but for most people they remain distant. A disrupted neighborhood grocery store or a grounded holiday flight is different. It brings the consequences home.

title: What Everyone Gets Wrong About Genocide
content:
Genocide, as set out in the UN’s 1948 convention, has a 26-word definition that has caused problems its authors probably never imagined. 

The convention sums up the crime thus: “Genocide means any of the following acts committed with intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnical, racial or religious group as such.” It then lists those acts, including killing or otherwise harming the group. 

But that apparently simple sentence contains a chain of ambiguities. Is Ukraine a genocide? Is Gaza? Or the October 7 attacks in Israel? Reaching back to the past, is it true to describe European or Arab slavers as guilty of genocide (if the convention had existed then)? 

The answer depends partly on interpretation. This is in vivid contrast to other war law, where meanings are clear. The International Criminal Court’s statute, for instance, has no problem explaining two of its core crimes: war crimes and Crimes Against Humanity. There are no ambiguities. No disputes. Everyone can understand them. But the third core crime is different. Genocide’s definition radiates uncertainty.
snippet: Genocide, as set out in the UN’s 1948 convention, has a 26-word definition that has caused problems its authors probably never imagined.
